newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch bond outlook remains bullish - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Dutch bond outlook remains bullish - analysts.

text.p: The outlook for the Dutch bond market remains bullish despite a strong rally in the last month that has pushed yields to 1996 lows, analysts said.
They said yields would remain near current levels and could even dip further this year while the yield discount to German bunds, the widest in more than two years, holds.
A major factor is the fall in Dutch government bond supply as the Finance Ministry loses its thirst for borrowing.
"They hardly need any more money," said Niels Kortleve, fixed-income analyst at Rabobank International.
The ministry said last Monday it would not issue any new bonds in the fourth quarter of 1996, confirming expectations raised by the government's 1997 budget published last month.
The 1997 borrowing requirement is now forecast at about 22.5 billion guilders, down from an expected 35.1 billion in 1996 and 52.8 billion actually raised in 1995.
The tighter funding calendar is a result of lower redemptions of bonds and use of an obsolete cash reserve at the central bank to meet part of the government's funding commitments.
In response, yields on 10-year Dutch state loans have fallen about 40 basis points to 5.86 percent on Friday.
The yield discount to bunds also widened to 15 basis points, the widest margin since early 1994, although it came back in to about 10 basis points on Friday.

ABN AMRO senior bond strategist Gerlof de Vrij said he did not expect any new bond issues in the first quarter of 1997 as the authorities tried to counteract "front loading", the process followed in the past of issuing bonds early in the year.
"They have large coupon payments in the first half (of the year). They want to redress that," he said.
He said the outlook for guilder bonds was positive, but a revival of economic growth would choke off further price gains.
ABN AMRO said in a report issued this month that it no longer expected the yield differential with Germany to disappear in 1996, adding that Dutch benchmark bonds were now scarce.
It also cited expectations inflation would rise less than previously forecast, the positive response of financial markets to the budget and the smaller funding programme.
Rabobank's Kortleve does not expect any long Dutch bonds to be issued next year because, with the yield curve so steep, the ministry can cut interest payments by borrowing shorter term.
He said bond issuance would also be limited by increasing use of Dutch Treasury Certificates (DTCs).
DTCs are debt instruments maturing in less than one year.
Shorter borrowing would help the Dutch cut debt in the run-up to a single European currency and would mark a change in the policy of extending the duration of debt.
Korlteve said he did not expect a correction in the Dutch bond market, forecasting that the Bundesbank would keep German interest rates at current levels this year.
He sees scope for yields in the Netherlands and Germany to fall by another 25 to 30 basis points.
"We are bullish on the Netherlands because we are bullish on Germany," he said.
ING Barings is now more bullish on the Dutch market, having recently lowered its forecast of 10-year yields in one month's time to 5.80 percent from 6.20 percent.
"The picture is looking structurally very good for Dutch bonds," said an ING Barings analyst.
Dutch bank F. van Lanschot Bankiers has benefitted from the scarcity of state debt, last week increasing its October 2006 guilder bond issue to 350 million from 300 million.
"That was because the whole issue was placed in 20 minutes," said a spokesman for lead manager Rabobank International.
